## Finding

**Yes — model family measurably affects performance on Adult, but the effect is modest for any reasonable family.**

| family | CV AUC (train) | test AUC | test AP | acc | Brier |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| hist_gbm | 0.9291 ± 0.0014 | **0.9274** | 0.825 | 0.872 | 0.089 |
| random_forest | 0.9184 ± 0.0015 | 0.9188 | 0.810 | 0.869 | 0.093 |
| mlp | 0.9100 ± 0.0025 | 0.9125 | 0.785 | 0.860 | 0.098 |
| decision_tree | 0.9051 ± 0.0015 | 0.9076 | 0.785 | 0.858 | 0.098 |
| logreg_l2 | 0.9063 ± 0.0027 | 0.9065 | 0.769 | 0.853 | 0.101 |
| linear_svm | 0.9060 ± 0.0026 | 0.9064 | 0.769 | 0.854 | 0.101 |
| knn | 0.8988 ± 0.0033 | 0.8992 | 0.750 | 0.849 | 0.105 |
| gaussian_nb | 0.8631 ± 0.0034 | 0.8600 | 0.652 | 0.751 | 0.241 |

Key numbers (paired bootstrap over held-out test rows, 2000 resamples):

- **HistGBM − LogReg = +0.0209** [+0.0179, +0.0240] — the headline metric
- HistGBM − RandomForest = +0.0086 [+0.0065, +0.0108]
- LogReg − LinearSVM = +0.0001 [−0.0005, +0.0007] (indistinguishable)
- LogReg − DecisionTree = −0.0011 [−0.0049, +0.0026] (indistinguishable)

Two things make the "meaningfully" judgment concrete. The spread across the seven mainstream families (0.028 AUC) is **~13× the mean within-family CV noise** (sd ≈ 0.0022), so the ordering is not sampling noise — and the ranking reproduced exactly under an independent repeated 5×2-fold CV on the full data (HGB − LogReg = +0.0228 there vs +0.0209 on test). But the *practical* size is small: boosting buys ~2 AUC points and ~2 accuracy points over a plain regularised linear model, and a well-tuned single decision tree ties logistic regression. The one genuinely large gap is Gaussian naive Bayes (−0.067 AUC, badly miscalibrated at Brier 0.241), which fails because its independence assumption and Gaussian likelihood are wrong for one-hot categoricals and the spiky capital-gain distribution.

Interpretation: this is a tabular dataset with strong main effects and moderate interactions, so linear models capture most of the signal and boosting adds a real but bounded increment.

Caveats worth flagging: I could not test XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost (not installed) or an RBF-kernel SVM (cost), so "boosting" is represented only by sklearn's HistGradientBoosting. Headline test numbers use a single 80/20 split seed; split variability was addressed with the repeated-CV replication rather than by repeating the full tuning pipeline across many seeds. No imbalance handling was applied — that would move the accuracy/F1 columns but not the AUC ranking.

Files written: `analysis.py`, `result.json`, plus supporting `comparison.json` and `robustness.json`.

parsed_result.summary: Yes, but the effect is real rather than large. With tuning and identical preprocessing, gradient-boosted trees (HistGradientBoosting) are the best family at test ROC-AUC 0.927, beating regularised logistic regression (0.907) by 0.021 AUC (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.018, 0.024]) and random forest (0.919) by 0.009. The full ordering is hist_gbm > random_forest > MLP > decision tree ~ logistic regression ~ linear SVM > kNN >> Gaussian naive Bayes; the spread across the seven mainstream families (0.028 AUC) is about 13x the within-family CV noise (sd ~0.002), so family choice matters statistically, but every non-naive-Bayes family lands within ~3 AUC points of the best.
parsed_result.primary_metric_name: ROC-AUC difference (HistGradientBoosting - Logistic Regression) on held-out test set
parsed_result.direction: HistGBM > RF > MLP > Tree ~ LogReg ~ LinearSVM > kNN >> GaussianNB; boosting wins by a small but statistically unambiguous margin
parsed_result.methodological_choices: DATA: dropped 52 exact duplicate rows (to prevent identical records straddling the split) and dropped the string 'education' column as a redundant re-encoding of 'education-num'; kept 'fnlwgt' (a census sampling weight, often discarded as noise); missing workclass/occupation/native-country treated as an explicit '__missing__' category rather than imputed or row-dropped. ENCODING: one-hot (min_frequency=10, unknowns ignored) + standardised numerics for logistic regression, linear SVM, kNN, MLP, Gaussian NB, decision tree and random forest; ordinal encoding with HistGradientBoosting's native categorical splits for the booster - i.e. each family got its conventional representation rather than one forced common matrix. SPLIT: single stratified 80/20 train/test (seed 0); hyperparameters chosen by 3-fold stratified CV grid search on the training set only (small grids: LogReg C; LinearSVC C, Platt-calibrated for probabilities; kNN k/weights; tree depth/leaf size; RF min_samples_leaf/max_features with 400 trees; MLP width/alpha with early stopping; HGB learning rate/leaves/leaf size with early stopping). METRIC: ROC-AUC as primary (threshold-free, robust to the 24/76 imbalance); average precision, accuracy/F1 at a fixed 0.5 threshold, Brier and log loss as secondary - accuracy and AP give the same ranking. INFERENCE: paired stratified bootstrap (2000 resamples) over the held-out test rows so all models are scored on the same resample; between-family gaps were also reproduced independently by repeated 5x2-fold CV over the full dataset with the selected configs (HGB - LogReg = +0.0228 there vs +0.0209 on test). NO imbalance handling (no class weights, resampling, or threshold tuning) - a different researcher weighting classes or tuning thresholds would change the accuracy/F1 columns though not materially the AUC ranking. Families NOT tested for cost reasons: kernel (RBF) SVM, and XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost (unavailable in this environment), so 'best boosting implementation' is represented only by sklearn's HistGradientBoosting. Only one train/test seed was used for the headline test-set numbers; split-to-split variability was addressed via the repeated-CV check rather than by repeating the whole tuning pipeline over many seeds.
